events.title: Neolithic Settlement
events.description: Archaeological evidence shows human settlement in present-day Niger during the Neolithic period. The Sahara region was then more humid, supporting agricultural and pastoral development. Rock art and archaeological sites prove the existence of early hunter-gatherer societies and their later transition to agricultural societies. These early inhabitants were ancestors of modern Niger's various ethnic groups.

events.title: Beginning of Sahara Desertification
events.description: Climate change led to the beginning of Sahara desertification, forcing populations to migrate south to more habitable Sahel regions. This process continued for thousands of years, forming present-day Niger's population distribution pattern. The north gradually became the domain of nomadic peoples, while the south developed into agricultural areas.

events.title: Iron Age Culture
events.description: The Niger region entered the Iron Age, with mastery of iron-working technology promoting increased agricultural productivity and social organization complexity. Archaeological discoveries show specialized blacksmiths and potters existed, with increasingly clear social division of labor. This period laid the technological foundation for later kingdom emergence.

events.title: Hausa City-States Prosperity
events.description: The Hausa city-states reached their peak during this period, controlling important trade routes, particularly commercial paths connecting North Africa and West African forest zones. Kano and Katsina became important commercial centers, famous for textiles, leather goods, and metalwork. Islam spread widely among the ruling classes.

events.title: Tuareg Southern Migration
events.description: The Berber Tuareg people migrated south from northern desert regions, establishing several sultanates in central-northern Niger, including the Sultanate of Agadez. The Tuareg controlled key segments of trans-Saharan trade, particularly salt and slave trade, becoming important regional political forces.

events.title: Political Fragmentation and Competition
events.description: The Niger region fragmented into numerous small kingdoms and chieftaincies, including Hausa city-states, Tuareg sultanates, and various tribal alliances. These political entities frequently engaged in wars and conflicts, competing for control of trade routes. The slave trade reached its peak during this period.

events.title: Early Trade Route Establishment
events.description: Trans-Saharan trade routes began forming, with the Niger region becoming an important transit point due to its strategic location. Caravans carrying salt, gold, ivory, and slaves crossed the Sahara, promoting cultural and economic exchange between regions. These trade routes provided the economic foundation for later city-state prosperity.

events.title: Rise of Kanem-Bornu Empire
events.description: In the Lake Chad region, the powerful Kanem-Bornu Empire began to rise, extending its influence to eastern Niger. This empire controlled important trade routes, particularly commercial paths connecting Central and North Africa. Imperial rule promoted political integration and economic development in the region.

events.title: Introduction of Islam
events.description: Through trans-Saharan trade, Islam began entering the Niger region. Muslim merchants and missionaries brought new religion, writing systems, and legal institutions. Islam first spread in cities and trading centers, then gradually expanded to rural areas, coexisting with local traditional beliefs.

events.title: Trans-Saharan Trade Flourishing
events.description: Trans-Saharan trade reached new heights, with Niger becoming a key corridor connecting North Africa and West African interior. Salt mines in places like Bilma became important sources of trade commodities. Camel caravans regularly crossed the Sahara, bringing goods, books, and Islamic culture from North Africa, exchanging for gold, slaves, and other West African products.

events.title: Rise of Hausa City-States
events.description: The Hausa people began establishing city-states in southern Niger, including the seven major city-states of Biram, Daura, Gobir, Kano, Katsina, Rano, and Zaria. These city-states were renowned for trade and craftsmanship, developing complex political and social systems. Hausa language became the regional lingua franca.

events.title: Mali Empire Influence
events.description: The prosperous Mali Empire under Mansa Musa reached its zenith, with its influence extending to western Niger. The empire controlled important cities like Gao, promoting the spread of Islamic scholarship and culture. Mali Empire's commercial networks further integrated the Niger region into the West African trade system.

events.title: Foundation of Agadez
events.description: The Tuareg people established the city of Agadez on the southern edge of the Sahara, becoming an important trading center and political power base. The city was strategically located on key routes connecting North Africa and Hausaland, developing into a major trans-Saharan trade hub. Agadez's architecture and culture blended Berber and Sahelian traditions.

events.title: Songhai Empire Expansion
events.description: The powerful Songhai Empire extended its influence to western Niger, controlling important cities along the Niger River. Songhai rule brought more unified administrative management and Islamic legal systems, promoting further regional trade development.

events.title: Impact of Moroccan Invasion
events.description: After Moroccan forces defeated the Songhai Empire, the political landscape of western Niger underwent major changes. Although Moroccans did not directly rule Niger, the Songhai Empire's collapse led to political fragmentation, creating opportunities for other forces to rise.

events.title: Usman dan Fodio's Jihad
events.description: Fulani religious leader Usman dan Fodio launched a jihad in Hausaland, establishing the Sokoto Caliphate. This jihad aimed to purify Islam and eliminate pagan customs. The Sokoto Caliphate became one of West Africa's largest political entities, with its influence extending to Niger's southern Hausa regions.

events.title: Sokoto Caliphate Rule
events.description: The Sokoto Caliphate ruled southern Niger for nearly a century, establishing a unified Islamic administrative system. The Caliphate promoted Islamic education, established numerous Quranic schools, and facilitated the spread of Arabic script. It also strengthened slavery and the slave trade.

events.title: Beginning of French Colonial Expansion
events.description: France began establishing colonial outposts in the Niger region, first building trading posts along the Niger River. France's goal was to connect its colonies in West and North Africa, with Niger's strategic position making it key to this plan.

events.title: Voulet-Chanoine Mission
events.description: French officer Paul Voulet led an expedition across Niger, meeting with British forces in the Lake Chad region, establishing French sovereignty claims over Niger. This mission was an important component of France's 'Atlantic to Red Sea' colonial plan.

events.title: European Explorers Arrive
events.description: European explorers like Heinrich Barth and Gustav Nachtigal began exploring the Niger region, mapping and recording local political, economic, and social conditions. These expeditions provided important intelligence for later colonial conquest.

events.title: French Colonial Conquest
events.description: French forces systematically conquered Niger's various regions, defeating local resistance forces. The conquest process included military actions against Hausa city-states, Tuareg sultanates, and other tribes. By 1922, France completely controlled Niger's territory, establishing a colonial administrative system.

events.title: Establishment of Zinder Military Territory
events.description: France established a military territory in Zinder as a base for controlling southern Niger and Hausa regions. This marked the beginning of France's systematic colonial rule over Niger. Colonial authorities began appointing local chiefs as tools of indirect rule while establishing French legal systems.

events.title: Incorporation into French West Africa
events.description: Niger officially became part of the French West Africa federation, with administrative center in Niamey. France implemented direct rule, introducing French law, education systems, and administrative structures. Traditional political structures were marginalized or completely destroyed.

events.title: Kaocen's Early Resistance
events.description: Tuareg leader Kaocen ag Mohamed organized the first large-scale armed resistance against French colonial rule. He united multiple Tuareg tribes in an attempt to expel the French and restore independence. Though ultimately defeated by French forces, this resistance demonstrated the strong will of local people.

events.title: Tuareg Uprising
events.description: The Tuareg people launched a large-scale uprising under leaders Kaocen and Firhoun, opposing French colonial rule. The uprising lasted several years, with France deploying significant military force to suppress it. This uprising demonstrated strong local resistance to colonial rule.

events.title: World War I Impact
events.description: During World War I, Niger was forced to contribute to France's war effort. Thousands of Nigeriens were conscripted and sent to European and African battlefields. Meanwhile, colonial government intensified material requisitions, leading to economic hardship and increased social discontent.

events.title: Great Tuareg Uprising
events.description: Under pressure from wartime conscription and taxation, the Tuareg launched their largest uprising under Kaocen's leadership. The rebellion briefly controlled vast areas of northern Niger, even threatening Agadez. France deployed substantial military forces and aircraft to finally suppress the uprising, with Kaocen killed in 1919.

events.title: Forced Labor and Taxation
events.description: The French colonial government implemented harsh forced labor systems and heavy taxation policies, requiring locals to work for the colonial government and French companies. These policies created enormous social and economic burdens, causing widespread discontent. Many people fled their homes to avoid forced labor.

events.title: Administrative Reorganization
events.description: After completing the conquest of Niger, France conducted comprehensive administrative reorganization. Several military and civil circles were established, appointing French administrators and local chiefs. This period also witnessed the consolidation of Niamey's status as the colonial capital.

events.title: Groundnut Cultivation Promotion
events.description: The French colonial government began vigorously promoting groundnut cultivation as an export cash crop. This changed Niger's agricultural structure, shifting many farmers from subsistence farming to cash crop production. While bringing some income, it also increased dependence on the colonial economic system and food security vulnerability.

events.title: Colonial Education System Establishment
events.description: France established French-language schools in major cities to train local elite classes. The education system aimed to create French-speaking, French culture-identifying local administrators. However, educational opportunities were extremely limited, with the vast majority of the population still unable to receive formal education.

events.title: Niger Becomes Separate Colony
events.description: Niger separated from the French West Africa federation to become an independent colony with its own governor. This administrative reform gave Niger greater autonomy but remained under strict French control.

events.title: Vichy France Rule
events.description: During World War II, Niger was under Vichy France rule. Economic difficulties intensified during this period, with increased forced labor and material requisitions. The war also exposed limitations of French power, planting seeds for later independence movements.

events.title: French Union Status
events.description: After the war, Niger gained overseas territory status within the French Union. The new constitution granted limited autonomy and established local assemblies. Though limited, this reform provided space for political participation and nationalist movement development.

events.title: Formation of Niger Progressive Party
events.description: Hamani Diori and others formed the Niger Progressive Party, becoming Niger's most important political organization. The party initially maintained close relations with France but gradually developed independent political positions, playing a key role in the independence movement.

events.title: Abolition of Forced Labor
events.description: In the post-war reform wave, France abolished forced labor systems in African colonies. This reform was widely welcomed in Niger, but economic transition also brought new challenges. Many infrastructure projects slowed due to labor shortages.

events.title: First Local Elections
events.description: Niger held its first local elections, allowing limited local political participation. Although suffrage was strictly restricted to only a few educated elites and chiefs, this marked the beginning of political modernization.

events.title: Formation of Sawaba Party
events.description: The radical Sawaba Party (Niger Democratic Union) was formed, led by Bakary Djibo. The party demanded immediate independence, taking more radical positions than the Progressive Party. Sawaba Party had connections to communist movements and was popular among unions and youth.

events.title: Internal Autonomy
events.description: Under France's Loi-Cadre, Niger gained internal autonomy status, establishing a semi-autonomous government. Hamani Diori became head of government, beginning preparations for complete independence. This reform accelerated the decolonization process.

events.title: French Community
events.description: In de Gaulle's constitutional referendum, Niger chose to join the French Community, gaining greater autonomy. This was an important step toward complete independence while maintaining special relations with France.

events.title: Niger Independence
events.description: Niger gained independence from France, with Hamani Diori becoming the first president. Independence celebrations were held in Niamey, marking the end of French colonial rule in Niger. Niger became a member of the United Nations and Organization of African Unity.

events.title: Diori's One-Party Rule
events.description: Hamani Diori established a one-party state, with the Niger Progressive Party becoming the only legal party. The government implemented pro-Western policies, maintaining close relations with France. Though politically stable, economic development was slow and social inequality increased.

events.title: Sahel Drought Disaster
events.description: Severe drought struck the Sahel region, with Niger severely affected. The drought caused massive famine, livestock deaths, and population migration. Government response was inadequate, international aid insufficient, causing hundreds of thousands of deaths. This disaster exposed government incompetence.

events.title: Seyni Kountché Military Coup
events.description: Lieutenant Colonel Seyni Kountché led a military coup, overthrowing Diori's government. The coup's background included drought crisis, economic difficulties, and political corruption. Kountché established a military government, promising reform and modernization.

events.title: Kountché's Military Rule
events.description: During Seyni Kountché's rule, a series of reforms were implemented, including land reform, education reform, and administrative modernization. The government adopted more independent foreign policies, establishing close relations with Libya. However, political freedom was restricted and opposition suppressed.

events.title: Discovery of Uranium Deposits
events.description: Large uranium deposits were discovered in the Arlit region, making Niger one of the world's major uranium producers. Uranium mining brought important revenue to the country but also caused environmental and social problems. French companies controlled most mining rights.

events.title: Economic Crisis
events.description: Niger faced severe economic crisis, including debt crisis, inflation, and rising unemployment. Drought and locust swarms exacerbated agricultural difficulties. The government was forced to implement austerity policies, cutting public spending, causing social discontent.

events.title: Ali Saibou Military Coup
events.description: Colonel Ali Saibou launched a military coup, overthrowing and killing Seyni Kountché. Saibou accused Kountché of corruption and economic mismanagement. The new government promised economic reform and political opening.

events.title: Beginning of Tuareg Rebellion
events.description: Northern Tuareg people began armed rebellion, demanding greater autonomy and development aid. The rebellion's roots included political marginalization, economic underdevelopment, and cultural oppression. This conflict would continue to trouble Niger for years.

events.title: National Conference
events.description: Under popular pressure, the government convened a national conference to discuss political reform. The conference decided to transition to multi-party democracy and draft a new constitution. This marked the beginning of Niger's democratization process.

events.title: Mahamane Ousmane Elected President
events.description: In Niger's first multi-party democratic election, Mahamane Ousmane was elected president. The new constitution established a multi-party democratic system, guaranteeing basic rights and freedoms. Ousmane's government was committed to democratic consolidation and economic reform.

events.title: Peace Agreement with Tuareg
events.description: The government signed a peace agreement with Tuareg rebels, ending five years of armed conflict. The agreement included weapon destruction, rebel integration, and northern development plans. However, the agreement's implementation was not entirely successful.

events.title: Ibrahim Baré Maïnassara Military Coup
events.description: Colonel Ibrahim Baré Maïnassara launched a military coup, overthrowing Ousmane's government. The coup's justification was political instability and economic difficulties. Maïnassara established a military government, suspending the constitution and party activities.

events.title: Maïnassara's Authoritarian Rule
events.description: Maïnassara implemented authoritarian rule, suppressing opposition and restricting media freedom. In 1996, he was elected president in a controversial election. The government faced international sanctions and domestic protests. Economic conditions showed no significant improvement.

events.title: Assassination of Maïnassara
events.description: President Maïnassara was killed by the presidential guard at Niamey airport. The assassination's motives included political disagreements and personal grudges. This event shocked the nation and led to political crisis.

events.title: Daouda Malam Wanké Elected President
events.description: In elections held after Maïnassara's assassination, Daouda Malam Wanké was elected president. Wanké promised to restore democratic institutions, promote reconciliation, and foster economic development. His election marked the restoration of democracy.

events.title: President Tandja Re-elected
events.description: Mamadou Tandja was re-elected in the presidential election. His second term faced new challenges, including food crisis, renewed Tuareg rebellion, and terrorist threats.

events.title: Food Crisis
events.description: Niger suffered a severe food crisis affecting millions of people. The crisis's causes included drought, locust swarms, and high grain prices. The international community provided emergency aid, but response measures were criticized as insufficient and delayed.

events.title: New Tuareg Rebellion
events.description: The north again erupted in Tuareg rebellion, led by the Niger Movement for Justice. Rebels complained that the 1995 peace agreement had not been adequately implemented, demanding greater autonomy and resource allocation. The conflict affected uranium mining.

events.title: New Peace Agreement with Tuareg
events.description: The government signed a new peace agreement with Tuareg rebels, promising increased northern investment, rebel integration into national forces, and greater local autonomy. The agreement temporarily eased tensions.

events.title: Salou Djibo Military Coup
events.description: Military officers launched a coup, overthrowing President Tandja for attempting to modify the constitution to extend his term. Coup leader Salou Djibo promised to restore democratic institutions and hold new elections.

events.title: Mahamadou Issoufou Elected President
events.description: In elections organized by the military government, Mahamadou Issoufou was elected president. The election was considered free and fair, marking the restoration of democratic institutions. Issoufou promised reform and reconciliation.

events.title: Mali Crisis Impact
events.description: The political crisis in neighboring Mali and activities of Islamic extremist groups seriously affected Niger. Large numbers of refugees flooded into Niger, increasing security threats. Niger supported international military intervention in Mali.

events.title: French Military Base
events.description: France established a military base in Niger as part of Sahel region counter-terrorism operations. The base's establishment strengthened Niger's security capabilities but also raised sovereignty concerns.

events.title: Boko Haram Attacks
events.description: Nigerian Islamic extremist group Boko Haram began launching attacks in southeastern Niger, causing massive civilian casualties. Niger's government declared a state of emergency, cooperating with neighbors to combat terrorism.

events.title: President Issoufou Re-elected
events.description: Mahamadou Issoufou was re-elected in the presidential election. His second term faced severe challenges, including terrorist threats, economic difficulties, and climate change impacts.

events.title: Joining G5 Sahel
events.description: Niger joined the G5 Sahel organization, cooperating with Mali, Burkina Faso, Chad, and Mauritania to combat terrorism and organized crime. This cooperation mechanism received support from France and the EU.

events.title: Presidential Election Controversy
events.description: The presidential election sparked controversy, with opposition alleging electoral fraud. Mohamed Bazoum was elected president, but election results were questioned. Political tensions escalated, triggering protests and violence.

events.title: Bazoum's Inauguration
events.description: Mohamed Bazoum was officially inaugurated as president, marking Niger's first democratic power transition in history. Bazoum promised to fight corruption, improve security conditions, and promote economic development.

events.title: Failed Coup Attempt
events.description: Just two days before Bazoum's inauguration, a failed military coup attempt occurred. The coup attempt was thwarted, and several officers were arrested. This event showed Niger's political fragility and military dissatisfaction.

events.title: Successful Military Coup
events.description: The presidential guard launched a coup, overthrowing Bazoum's government. Coup leader General Abdourahamane Tchiani announced the formation of the National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland. The coup's causes included security deterioration, economic difficulties, and political dissatisfaction.

events.title: ECOWAS Sanctions
events.description: The Economic Community of West African States imposed severe sanctions on Niger, including border closures, asset freezes, and threats of military intervention. Sanctions aimed to force the military government to restore democratic institutions but also exacerbated the humanitarian crisis.

events.title: Deteriorating Relations with France
events.description: The military government demanded France withdraw its ambassador to Niger and questioned France's military presence in Niger. This marked a major shift in Niger's relations with its former colonial power, reflecting rising anti-French sentiment.

events.title: French Military Withdrawal
events.description: France announced military withdrawal from Niger, ending its military presence in the country. The withdrawal marked further weakening of French influence in the Sahel region and created space for other international actors to enter the region.

events.title: Ongoing Political Crisis
events.description: Niger remains in political crisis, with the military government facing international isolation and economic sanctions. The security situation remains severe, with terrorist threats continuing. Humanitarian conditions have deteriorated, with millions needing assistance. The international community continues calling for restoration of democratic institutions, but the military government has not yet clarified a transition timeline. Niger's future is full of uncertainty, requiring joint efforts from all parties to seek peaceful solutions.
